exam: A patient presents with unilateral nasal obstruction and epistaxis; what is your next diagnostic step — endoscopic examination and biopsy to exclude malignancy.
How does a septal hematoma lead to a saddle‑nose deformity if untreated — cartilage necrosis from loss of perichondrial blood supply.
Differentiate anterior from posterior epistaxis in a low‑resource setting — location of bleeding, response to anterior packing, need for arterial ligation.
What clinical features suggest chronic rhinosinusitis rather than acute viral rhinitis — symptoms >12 weeks, facial pain, nasal discharge, CT changes.
Why is nasal irrigation recommended in post‑viral rhinitis — it restores mucociliary clearance without systemic drugs.
In a trauma patient with clear nasal discharge, what test confirms CSF leak — β‑2 transferrin assay; if unavailable, glucose testing is less reliable.
Explain why olfactory loss is an early sign in COVID‑19 — virus binds ACE2 receptors on nasal epithelium, impairing olfactory neurons.
What are the contraindications to using topical decongestant sprays long‑term — risk of rhinitis medicamentosa and rebound congestion.
ai.title: Nasal Cavity Anatomy and Clinical Relevance
ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The nasal cavity is a paired air‑filled space that conditions inhaled air and houses the olfactory mucosa. Understanding its anatomy guides diagnosis of common infections, trauma, and tumors, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: Air is warmed, humidified, and filtered.
Olfaction occurs on the superior concha and upper septum.
sections.p: The nasal cavity extends from the nostrils to the choanae and is divided by the nasal septum. It is lined by respiratory mucosa and, superiorly, by olfactory epithelium.

b: Three bony conchae increase surface area.
sections.p: Each cavity is a pyramidal space bounded laterally by the nasal conchae (superior, middle, inferior) and medially by the septum (bone and cartilage). The roof is formed by the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone.

b: Cribriform plate → risk of CSF leak with trauma.
Middle meatus → drainage of maxillary, frontal, anterior ethmoid sinuses.
sections.p: Superiorly the cavity contacts the anterior cranial fossa; posteriorly it opens into the nasopharynx; laterally it is adjacent to the maxillary sinus and orbit.

b: Epistaxis often originates from Kiesselbach’s plexus (anterior septum).
sections.p: Arterial blood comes from branches of the internal and external carotid arteries, chiefly the sphenopalatine artery (branch of maxillary) and the anterior ethmoidal artery.

b: Loss of smell suggests olfactory nerve or mucosal disease.
sections.p: Sensory innervation is via the trigeminal nerve (V2 – maxillary branch) for the mucosa and V1 – ophthalmic branch for the superior part. Olfactory nerves (CN I) pass through the cribriform plate to the olfactory bulb.

b: Cilia beat at ~12 mm/min; impaired in chronic rhinosinusitis.
sections.p: The cavity filters particles, humidifies air, and provides the sense of smell. The mucociliary clearance system moves mucus toward the nasopharynx.

b: Acute rhinitis: viral, often self‑limited; treat symptomatically.
Chronic rhinosinusitis: >12 weeks of symptoms, CT needed if surgery considered.
Nasal polyps: associated with asthma, aspirin‑exacerbated respiratory disease.
sections.p: Common problems include acute rhinitis, chronic rhinosinusitis, epistaxis, nasal polyps, and malignancy (e.g., olfactory neuroblastoma). Trauma can cause septal hematoma, CSF leak, or orbital injury.

t.b: Visualises mucosa, polyps, or tumor; guides biopsy.
Assesses sinus opacification, bony erosion; essential before surgery.
Stops anterior epistaxis; compresses Kiesselbach’s plexus.

b: Septal hematoma presents as a soft, fluctuant swelling; drain promptly to prevent cartilage necrosis.
CSF leak: clear, watery drainage that tests positive for β‑2 transferrin.
sections.p: Inspection: external deformity, septal deviation. Palpation: tenderness over frontal sinus. Anterior rhinoscopy: assess septum, turbinates, bleeding source. Endoscopic exam if available.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe facial swelling with vision loss
Persistent fever and facial pain >10 days suggesting complicated sinusitis
